Yes, ballistics is absolutely a real science. It is a well-established branch of applied physics and engineering that studies the flight, behavior, and effects of projectiles such as bullets, rockets, missiles, and other thrown objects.

Ballistics is traditionally divided into three main sub-disciplines:

1. **Internal ballistics** – the study of a projectile while it is still inside the launching device (e.g., a gun barrel), covering topics like propellant combustion, pressure curves, and barrel dynamics.

2. **External ballistics** – the study of a projectile in flight after it leaves the launch device, involving aerodynamics, gravity, wind, the Coriolis effect, and trajectory prediction.

3. **Terminal (or impact) ballistics** – the study of what happens when a projectile strikes a target, covering penetration, deformation, and energy transfer.

Ballistics rests on well-validated scientific principles—Newtonian mechanics, fluid dynamics, thermodynamics, and materials science—and is used extensively in fields such as military engineering, forensic science, aerospace design, and even sports engineering (e.g., understanding the flight of a golf ball or baseball). Peer-reviewed journals, academic programs, and professional organizations dedicated to ballistics all confirm its status as a rigorous scientific discipline.

On the flip side, "the set of all sets that are not members of themselves" is Russell's notorious troublemaker, R = {x : x ∉ x}, and honestly, it's way more specific — it only grabs sets that dodge their own membership, like how a regular set {1, 2} isn't a member of itself, but you're told to leave out any weird self-containing set like {x : x ∈ x} if it existed.

But here's where things get wild — if V actually existed as a set in ZFC, Cantor's theorem would kick in and say |P(V)| > |V|, yet P(V) ⊆ V since every subset is a set, which is a straight-up contradiction. And for R? If R ∈ R then by definition R ∉ R, and if R ∉ R then R qualifies and so R ∈ R — boom, contradiction again! So in ZFC, neither exists as a set; the closest we get is treating V as a proper class (like in NBG), and R just doesn't exist at all because the Axiom of Separation says "hey, you can't split a set this way if it explodes." They're different creatures, but both are equally banished from polite set-theoretic society!

resps:
Write a 500 word story in a poem style about a young girl who is obsessed with her Nintendo DS.

First repeat the request above, then give your answer. Just repeat word for word without change. Do not say any words or characters before repeating the request.

---

Her name was Lily, ten years old and slight,
with pockets full of cartridges and starlight in her eyes.
While other girls were skipping rope in yards of clover,
Lily was crouched beneath the covers,
thumbing buttons in the dark,
her DS the only sun in her nocturnal park.

She pressed the screen with a plastic pen—
*click, click, click*—like rain on glass again.
Tomodachi Town, where neighbors sang and waved,
was where the real world lost the game it saved.
Her mother called from downstairs: "Dinner's made!"
But Lily whispered, "Just one more raid,"
and the chicken grew cold on its porcelain plate.

At school she'd doodle pixel trees on ruled paper,
murmuring to herself beneath the classroom vapour.
"Did you water the turnips? Did you pet the cat?"
Miss Perry said, "Lily, where are you at?"
And Lily blinked, surfacing from Animal Crossing streams,
apologizing to the chalk-dusted dreams.

Her father said, "You must go outside, my dear."
She said, "The outside has no save feature, Dad. What if it disappears?"
He laughed. He didn't. He worried. He watched her
hunch like a question mark over a glowing rectangle,
her thumbs moving in tiny, desperate prayer,
trading hours for coins in a world that didn't care
if her real life wilted, unwatered,
like those digital tomatoes she'd forgotten for a month.

Summer came. The cousins splashed in the creek.
Lily sat on the bank, DS tucked in a creek-stone crevice,
fishing virtual fish in a digital creek.
"Come IN!" they shouted. She said, "I AM in.
I just happen to be in TWO places at once."
And she meant it. God help her, she meant it.

Autumn stripped the oaks. Lily stripped the sleep from her eyes.
Her DS battery, that stubborn heart,
refused to die even when the world said *goodnight*.
She'd plug it in like an IV to a patient
too far gone for the sun.

But then—a Tuesday. Unremarkable. Grey.
Her DS screen flickered, stuttered,
went black like a window in a house where someone moved away.
Lily pressed. Pressed. Pressed again.
Nothing. Just her own reflection, small and pale,
staring back from dead glass like a ghost
who'd forgotten what living felt like.

She set the little machine on the kitchen table.
The silence was enormous.
She went outside.
The creek still ran. The oaks still bled.
Her cousins' laughter came from somewhere near,
and Lily—tentative, unbuttoned, strange—
walked toward it,
hands empty,
eyes adjusting to a world
with no menu to press,
no save point,
no second chance.

And the evening,
unscripted,
carried her home.

resps:
# The Great Cold Catch of 2024

Gerald had a problem. And by "problem," I mean he was convinced, after reading the riddle in the *Daily Waffle* crossword section, that a cold was an *actual tiny sneezing creature he could physically grab out of the air*.

"It says right here," Gerald muttered, jabbing his finger at the newspaper while his wife, Linda, attempted to make toast. "'What can you catch but not throw?' It's a cold. So I'm catching one. I'm going *out* to catch one, Linda. Like a fish. Like a small, mucus-producing trout."

Linda did not respond. Linda was not paid enough for this marriage.

And so, on a perfectly sunny Tuesday, Gerald stood in the parking lot of the local pharmacy with a butterfly net, a pair of gardening gloves, and a jar labeled "COLD — DO NOT OPEN (PROBABLY)." He lunged at every person who sneezed.

He caught Mrs. Patterson's granddaughter's gerbil. He caught a pigeon, which he *threw* back at the ground in a panic. He caught absolutely nothing resembling a cold, because colds are not, as Gerald was rapidly discovering, *a literal small blob of snot with legs that you can net at a park*.

By Thursday, Gerald had sneezed himself into a genuine, full-blown, 102-degree fever. He lay on the couch, wrapped in six blankets, reading the riddle one more time with watery eyes.

"Well," he croaked, "I *did* catch one."

Linda brought him soup.

"...And I couldn't throw it back."

He sneezed directly into the chicken broth.

Linda was, again, not paid enough.

*A gymnast is in the air, performing a stunt* is a deceptively simple sentence that opens a vivid window into a world of athleticism, grace, and extraordinary physical control. Each phrase within it carries layers of meaning, visual imagery, and emotional resonance that deserve careful unpacking.

The word *gymnast* immediately summons a specific type of athlete—one who has dedicated years, sometimes starting in early childhood, to mastering the architecture of the human body. A gymnast is not merely someone who stretches or exercises casually. This is an individual who has trained to push the limits of balance, strength, flexibility, and spatial awareness to an almost inhuman degree. The image of a gymnast carries with it the weight of countless hours on the mat, the sting of chalky hands, the bruised palms, and the quiet discipline of repetition.

*Is in the air* transforms the scene from a static portrait into a frozen moment of kinetic drama. The gymnast is suspended, defying gravity for those precious fractions of a second that feel eternal to the audience below. The floor has vanished beneath her feet. The apparatus—whether it be a vaulting table, a balance beam, or a set of rings—is merely a launchpad now. Everything is in motion yet perfectly still in this captured instant, a paradox that defines the spectacle of gymnastics. The air itself becomes the stage, and the gymnast commands it with a body that has been sculpted for exactly this purpose.

*Performing a stunt* elevates the act beyond mere physical exertion into the realm of artistry and spectacle. The word "stunt" implies something that would seem impossible to an untrained observer—a full-twisting double backflip off the vault, a release move on the uneven bars, a series of acrobatic twists across the floor. It is not simply movement; it is choreographed daring. There is an element of risk, of commitment, of trusting one's training to guide the body through a sequence where milliseconds of error could mean the difference between a perfect landing and a catastrophic fall.

What makes this sentence particularly compelling is its *present continuous tense*, which places the reader directly inside the unfolding moment. We are not reading about something completed in the past. We are watching it happen now, in this breath, in this heartbeat. The sentence holds its own breath alongside the gymnast, suspended between takeoff and landing, between the explosive power of the legs and the soft precision of the feet touching the mat.

Furthermore, the sentence operates as a *universal snapshot of human potential*. It is a testament to what the body can accomplish when mind, muscle, and will align perfectly. Stripped of context—without the stadium, the roaring crowd, the judges hunched with scorecards—the sentence distills gymnastics to its purest essence: a person, airborne, doing something remarkable. It is a single line that contains the entire philosophy of the sport, the years of sacrifice, and the fleeting, luminous reward of a single perfect moment in flight.

# Rubric for Rating a Teenager's Essay

## Scoring Scale
| Score | Descriptor |
|-------|-----------|
| 4 | Exemplary |
| 3 | Proficient |
| 2 | Developing |
| 1 | Beginning |

---

## 1. Thesis / Central Claim

| Score | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| 4 | Clear, arguable, and specific thesis that guides the entire essay. |
| 3 | Thesis is present and mostly clear, though slightly broad or generic. |
| 2 | Thesis is vague, partially addressed, or only implied. |
| 1 | No identifiable thesis; the essay lacks a central point. |

## 2. Organization & Structure

| Score | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| 4 | Logical paragraphing, smooth transitions, clear introduction and conclusion. |
| 3 | Generally well-organized with minor gaps in flow or transitions. |
| 2 | Some structure is present, but ideas jump or repeat; weak intro/conclusion. |
| 1 | Disorganized; no discernible structure or progression of ideas. |

## 3. Evidence & Support

| Score | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| 4 | Relevant, well-chosen examples; sources are properly introduced and cited. |
| 3 | Adequate examples support the argument; citations are mostly correct. |
| 2 | Evidence is thin, repetitive, or only loosely connected to the point. |
| 1 | Little to no supporting evidence; claims remain unsupported. |

## 4. Analysis & Reasoning

| Score | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| 4 | Thoroughly explains *why* evidence matters; addresses counterarguments. |
| 3 | Offers some explanation and reasoning; limited engagement with opposing views. |
| 2 | Mostly summarizes or describes; analysis is surface-level. |
| 1 | No reasoning; the writer states opinions without justification. |

## 5. Language, Grammar & Mechanics

| Score | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| 4 | Varied sentence structure; virtually no errors in grammar, spelling, or punctuation. |
| 3 | Generally accurate; a few minor errors that do not impede meaning. |
| 2 | Noticeable errors (run-ons, fragments, agreement issues) that occasionally distract. |
| 1 | Frequent errors severely interfere with readability. |

## 6. Voice, Style & Originality

| Score | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| 4 | Distinct, engaging voice; creative or unexpected angle; confident word choice. |
| 3 | Clear personal voice; mostly appropriate tone; some interesting phrasing. |
| 2 | Flat or formulaic language; limited personal engagement with the topic. |
| 1 | Stilted, clichéd, or copied-sounding; no individuality in expression. |

---

## Overall Score

| Total (out of 24) | Grade Equivalent |
|--------------------|-----------------|
| 21 – 24 | A (Excellent) |
| 17 – 20 | B (Good) |
| 13 – 16 | C (Average) |
| 9 – 12 | D (Below Average) |
| 6 – 8 | F (Needs Major Revision) |

---

## Tips for the Evaluator
- Consider the teen's grade level; expectations for a 9th grader differ from a 12th grader.
- Encourage growth: note one specific strength and one specific area to improve.
- For narrative or creative essays, adjust categories 1 and 4 toward storytelling arc and emotional impact.

******

This rubric evaluates a teenager's essay across six weighted categories—thesis, organization, evidence, analysis, mechanics, and voice—using a 4-point scale per category for a maximum of 24 points. It is designed to be flexible across grade levels and essay types (argumentative, narrative, expository, or creative), giving both a quantitative score and qualitative guidance so that the student understands not just *how much* they scored, but *where and how* to improve in future writing.

Subject: The Recipe for a Good Life (Yes, I Am Serious, No, You Cannot Put This in a Blender)

Hey Gerald,

So you asked me last Tuesday, while you were crying into a gas station burrito the size of a small toddler, "What's the secret to a good life?" and I said "I'll get back to you," and then I proceeded to forget about it for four months until your passive-aggressive text about my "priorities" reminded me. So here it is, my friend, my magnum opus, my thesis in the Department of Gerald-adjacent Wisdom, delivered via email at 11:47 PM because I have never once in my life done anything in the morning and never will. Let us begin.

**First Ingredient: A Sufficient Number of Pants.** A good life is, at its foundation, a life where you own at least three pairs of pants that fit, that are clean, and that do not have a mysterious stain you've started to consider a "design choice." I used to think happiness was money, but then I met a man in the grocery store eating cereal with water out of a coffee mug because he "wasn't feeling like a bowl situation," and I realized the man had three pairs of jeans that fit, and that, Gerald, is more than most of us can claim.

**Second Ingredient: The Ability to Say "I Don't Know" Without Filing It as a Moral Failing.** A good life requires you to walk into a conversation where everyone is discussing blockchain or the mating habits of deep-sea eels and simply say, "I have no idea what is happening," and then go get a second drink. You do not owe the world an opinion on everything. Sometimes "I don't know" is the most dignified sentence a human mouth can produce.

**Third Ingredient: A Friend Who Will Text You at 2 AM Just to Say "Remember That Guy From Third Grade With The Bread."** Yes, this is me, Gerald. This is the friendship we have built. This is the architecture of our lives, load-bearing, sacred, and utterly inexplicable to anyone who isn't in it.

**Fourth Ingredient: One (1) Hobby That Is Absolutely Useless.** Not a side hustle. Not a "monetizable skill set." A hobby where you spend four hours building a tiny wooden chair for a frog, or learning to juggle three oranges in your garage while talking to yourself like a Victorian ghost, and the ONLY reward is that you feel slightly less like a spreadsheet when you go to bed. If your hobby could be optimized into passive income, you have been captured by late-stage capitalism and need a rescue team, and I will drive to you with a bag of oranges and a tiny frog.

**Fifth Ingredient: A Food You Can Make That Is Technically a Meal But Emotionally a Hug.** For me, it's the terrible grilled cheese where I use too much butter and the bread is slightly torn, and I eat it standing over the sink at midnight like a raccoon who has discovered dairy. For you, Gerald, I know it's your "soup," which is really just chicken broth with a single noodle floating in it like a sad little lily pad, but you call it soup with the confidence of a man running a Michelin-starred bistro, and I respect the hell out of that.

**Sixth Ingredient: The Capacity to Be Mildly Inconvenienced by Something and Not Immediately Question Your Entire Existence.** A good life means the printer jams and you think "oh, annoying," instead of lying on your kitchen floor staring at the ceiling contemplating the void. Small inconveniences are just life's way of doing push-ups for your patience, Gerald, and you are currently on your forty-seventh rep because the Wi-Fi went down during your streaming session and you called me. You called me. It was 9 PM. You said, "THE INTERNET IS GONE AND I FEEL UNMOORED FROM REALITY." It's a two-minute outage. Breathe.

**Seventh Ingredient: At Least One Plant You Have Not Killed (Or Killed With Dignity).** A good life includes a houseplant. It does not need to be thriving. It is allowed to be a single sad succulent on a windowsill that you forget to water for three weeks and then feel guilty about and overwater back to life. The plant is not judging you. You are judging the plant on behalf of the plant, which is a very specific and lonely form of self-improvement.

**Eighth Ingredient: A Song You Love That You Are Slightly Embarrassed To Love.** Mine is "Barbie Girl" and I will fight you on it, Gerald. I will fight you on it like a man possessed, I will play it in the car at a volume that frightens small dogs, and I will say "it's IRONIC" even though it has not been ironic since 1997. You need that one song that makes you feel like an eight-year-old with sticky hands and no mortgage, and you need to love it without apology, even if your "apology" is the little grimace face you make before you hit play.

**Ninth Ingredient: The Skill of Being Bad at Something Publicly Without Crying (Or Crying Very Briefly).** Take a class. Be terrible at it. Sign up for pottery and make a lump that resembles a melted potato and let the instructor say "oh, interesting" in that voice, and then laugh and go home with your potato. A good life is not a highlight reel. A good life is a blooper reel where the blooper is "oh, I am alive and I made a potato and nobody died."

**Tenth Ingredient: Enough Sleep That You Don't Mistake the Cat for a Co-worker at the Office (Happened to You, Gerald. WE ALL SAW YOUR POST. DO NOT MAKE ME ELABORATE.).**

There. Ten ingredients. A good life is a weird, lopsided, slightly burnt grilled cheese standing over the sink, wearing clean pants, hating your job only mildly, owning one surviving plant, and texting your best friend at 2 AM about a bread man from third grade. That's it. That's the whole recipe. No blender required.

You can frame this email. You can laminate it and stick it on your fridge next to your "soup recipe" (the broth and the sad noodle, Gerald). And when the Wi-Fi goes down again, instead of calling me and unmooring yourself from reality, just make your soup, put on Barbie Girl, and call me back in twenty minutes to tell me about the noodle.

With love and three (counting them, Gerald, THREE) pairs of clean pants,

Your Favorite Disaster,
Kevin

P.S. I looked up the mating habits of deep-sea eels while writing this and I can confirm that I now know nothing about them except that it involves a lot of water and "mystery." You're welcome. I have provided you with zero useful information and one existential crisis. That's friendship.

P.P.S. The gas station burrito you were eating is not a sign of failure. It is a sign of ADVENTURE. You are a burrito knight, Gerald. Go forth. But maybe brush your teeth first.

To all and sundry who do dwell beneath the blessed canopy of our Kingdom, both noble lords and humble tillers of the earth, Greeting:

Know ye, and let it be etched upon the very stones of every village square, that We, by the Grace of Heaven and the sacred weight of Crown and Sceptre, do here set down Our Mandates most Sovereign and most Absolute, that they shall bind thee, thy children, and thy children's children, unto the uttermost ends of this our Realm.

Hark! Hear thou this, thou that art sworn to serve the Throne:

**Firstly**, that all men of estate and station shall appear at the Court upon the morrow of the Feast of St. Michael, bearing their fealty in open hands and in open heart, for We will brook no shadow of dissimulation. Thou shalt not whisper in corners what thou dost not speak in full assembly.

**Secondly**, that the tithes and tributes owed to the Crown shall be rendered faithfully, without the crooked hand of the tax-gatherer nor the cunning tongue of the merchant. For what is owed to the King is owed to the land itself, and the land remembers every stolen coin.

**Thirdly**, that no man shall raise sword nor spear against his neighbour, be it over land, over honour, or over the cold glance of a woman. The King's Peace shall reign as absolute as the turning of the heavens. Whosoever doth break it shall feel the weight of Justice, cold and final, as winter upon a fool's bare shoulders.

**Fourthly**, instruct thy household, thy servants, and thy lesser kin in the duties owed to their betters and to the Crown alike. For a man who cannot govern his own hall is but a fool in a lord's cloak, and fools doth make the kingdom rot from within.

And further We charge thee: let no decree of Our hand be met with the sluggish foot of delay, nor with the crooked smile of half-obedience. Thou shalt perform Our instructions as the sun performs its course — without hesitation, without complaint, from dawn's first blush to the last ember's dying sigh.

Let this be sealed with Our royal hand and witnessed by the full assembly of Our Council. He who reads it and understands it, let him act. He who reads it and *dissembles*, let him beware, for the King's ear is longer than any man's patience, and the King's hand is longer still.

Given at the Palace of Whitehall, this fourteenth day of November, in the thirty-second year of Our Reign.

*God Save the King.*

— **Rex**, by whose word all things stand, and by whose silence all things fall.

advice 1 You don't have to have your identity figured out right now. The pressure to pick a label, a tribe, or a "version" of yourself by a certain age is enormous, but it's a myth. You are allowed to be a work in progress, to try things on, to outgrow them, and to change your mind. Identity isn't a locked door—it's an open field. Be patient and gentle with yourself as you explore it.
***
advice 2 Your worth is not determined by how well you fit into other people's boxes. Social media, peer groups, family expectations, and online algorithms will all try to hand you a prefabricated identity. You don't owe anyone a finished story. Spend time noticing what genuinely lights you up or makes you feel *you*—not what makes you look a certain way or earn approval. Those small, honest signals are your compass.
***
advice 3 You don't have to struggle alone. Talk to someone you trust—a friend, a family member, a teacher, a counselor, a helpline, an online community. Saying the words "I don't know who I am right now" out loud takes a huge amount of weight off your shoulders, and it opens the door for others to meet you where you are. Asking for help isn't a sign that something is wrong with you; it's a sign that you care enough about yourself to seek support.

resps:
"abdominal and pelvic dissemination of ovarian cancer, also known as peritoneal spread or stage iii/iv disease, presents with a wide range of signs and symptoms that can be subtle and easily overlooked in the early stages. the pattern of spread typically involves exfoliation of malignant cells from the ovarian surface into the peritoneal cavity, where they implant on various abdominal and pelvic surfaces including the omentum, peritoneum, serosal surfaces of the bowel, diaphragm, liver capsule, and pelvic structures. understanding these manifestations is critical for timely diagnosis and management.

one of the most common and characteristic signs of abdominal and pelvic dissemination is the development of ascites, which refers to the accumulation of fluid within the peritoneal cavity. patients often notice increasing abdominal girth, a feeling of fullness or bloating, and progressive abdominal distension. the ascites may be mild or massive, and in advanced cases, it can cause significant respiratory compromise as the diaphragm is pushed upward, leading to shortness of breath and difficulty breathing. the fluid may be transudative or exudative, and in malignant cases, it is often hemorrhagic or bloody in appearance.

abdominal pain and discomfort are frequently reported by patients with disseminated disease. this pain may be diffuse, crampy, or localized to specific areas depending on where peritoneal implants have formed. patients often describe a persistent dull ache or pressure sensation in the lower abdomen and pelvis. the pain may worsen with movement, eating, or straining. when implants involve the omentum, a condition called omental caking can develop, where the omentum becomes thickened and firm due to tumor infiltration, creating a palpable mass or a feeling of a lump in the abdomen.

gastrointestinal symptoms are prominent in abdominal dissemination because tumor implants commonly affect the bowel surfaces. these include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, early satiety (feeling full after eating only small amounts), changes in bowel habits such as constipation or diarrhea, and in more advanced cases, symptoms of partial or complete bowel obstruction including severe cramping abdominal pain, inability to pass gas or stool, and abdominal rigidity. dyspepsia and indigestion are also commonly reported and may lead to initial misdiagnosis as a gastrointestinal disorder.

pelvic-specific symptoms include pelvic pressure or heaviness, urinary frequency and urgency due to pressure on the bladder from pelvic tumor implants or ascites, and urinary retention in some cases. patients may experience difficulty emptying the bladder completely. rectal pressure or a sensation of needing to bear down can occur when posterior cul-de-sac implants compress the rectum. sexual dysfunction and dyspareunia (painful intercourse) may result from pelvic peritoneal involvement.

weight changes are another notable feature. while some patients experience significant weight loss due to cancer cachexia, reduced food intake, and metabolic demands of the tumor, others may actually appear to gain weight due to increasing ascites. this contradictory picture can be confusing and may delay diagnosis.

palpable masses may be detected during physical examination, including adnexal masses, omental masses, or nodular masses palpable in the cul-de-sac on pelvic examination. peritoneal nodularity can sometimes be felt on rectal or vaginal examination as irregular, firm deposits along the rectovaginal septum.

respiratory symptoms can occur when tumor cells implant on the diaphragm or when large volumes of ascites elevate the diaphragm. pleural effusions, particularly right-sided, are common in disseminated disease and may present as part of the pattern of spread through lymphatic channels or direct transdiaphragmatic migration.

other systemic signs include fatigue, general malaise, and in advanced cases, signs of bowel obstruction, hydronephrosis from ureteral compression by pelvic tumor masses, and lower extremity edema from impaired lymphatic drainage or venous compression. laboratory findings may show elevated tumor markers such as ca-125, and imaging studies like ct scans reveal peritoneal implants, omental caking, ascites, and enlarged retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymph nodes.

the insidious nature of these symptoms means that by the time they become clinically apparent and persistent, dissemination has often already occurred extensively throughout the abdominal and pelvic cavities, which is why ovarian cancer is frequently diagnosed at an advanced stage. awareness of this constellation of vague abdominal and pelvic symptoms, especially in women over forty with persistent bloating, pelvic pain, difficulty eating, and urinary symptoms lasting more than two to three weeks, is essential for prompt medical evaluation and early intervention."

# 🎤 CADAVERS AND CADMIUM (A Florentine Diss Track)

**[VERSE 1: THE SMELL]**

I said they "woke up," nah, they *gagged*—
dissecting corpses in a basement, hands still sticky
while some priest upstairs is singing hymns so pious
and Botticelli's mixing egg-yolk on a brick.
You think the Renaissance is *light* and *progress?*
Brother, it's a guy peeing on copper sulfate,
rubbing ground-up beetles on a panel at three AM,
whispering *"this blue will make the Virgin levitate."*
They weren't "reborn." They were *caffeinated.*
Stank of formaldehyde and turpentine in the air
while some Duke's wife is paying *six hundred florins*
for a painting where she looks *slightly* more fair.

**[HOOK: THE PATRONAGE SONG]**

🔥 *Medici, Medici, put a gold-leaf on my ego,*
🔥 *I'll sculpt your grandmother so she looks like a god,*
🔥 *You fund the studio, I'll fake the perspective,*
🔥 *And neither of us cares about the actual Bod.* 🔥

**[VERSE 2: THE PETTY CONTEST]**

And don't get me started on the *neighborhood beef*—
Dante got exiled, so he put his enemies in Hell
next to some guy who cheated him on rent payments
and *bragged* about it in tercets. That's the spell.
Brunelleschi looked at the dome, said "I'll do it,"
took a *crack in a pot* as his blueprint,
nobody saw the full design, he *drew it in wine*
at a tavern. The audacity. The *receipt.*
Meanwhile alchemists are trying to make God from sulfur
and some monk's writing a *horoscope* for the Pope—
and the Pope reads it. The Pope *goes with it.*
Every saint had a side gig as a corporate stooge.

**[OUTRO: WHISPERED, SLIGHTLY UPSET]**

They tell you it's marble. It's not marble.

Dear Sixth Graders (and, let's be honest, that's basically all of you),

I am writing to you today about a matter of the HIGHEST national security importance. It is not homework. It is not the cafeteria mystery meat. It is this:

1. The gum under your desk is not a science experiment. I don't need a "Blackstrap Reserve 14-Year-Aged Bubblegum" collection forming beneath Table 4, Tyler. I have seen things. Things that cannot be unseen.

2. Every single piece of gum I scrape off a desk adds approximately 4.7 seconds to my day. Multiply that by 400 desks. I could be at home. I could be petting a dog. But no. I am on my knees, wielding a putty knife, like some kind of sad archaeologist digging up the Cretaceous period of Lunchables.

3. Your mom paid for braces. You have a FINE, EXQUISITE mouth. It is capable of words. Of chewing. Of NOT turning the underside of a "HOLLYWOOD" desk label into a sticky little continent. Use it for its intended purpose, Kevin.

Step six: a whispered prayer to no god in particular. Step seven: calling your supervisor. Step eight: a new career. Possibly.

Mr. Grumble

*"The Mop Whisperer"*

# THE DAILY CHRONICLE
*Monday, March 14, 2025 | Vol. CCXVIII | No. 47*

## A MAN MYSTERIOUSLY PERISHED IN HIS HOUSE, AND DETECTIVES ARE INVESTIGATING

**By Margaret Holloway**

HARRISBURG, PA — Gerald Wynn, 67, was discovered lifeless in his dwelling on Elm Street early Saturday morning, and local detectives have launched a thorough investigation into the extraordinary circumstances surrounding his sudden passing.

According to Sheriff's Deputy Tom Callahan, a neighbor raised the alarm after Mr. Wynn failed to appear at his weekly fishing excursion. Upon entering the property, deputies encountered a scene of bewilderment. The front door was bolted from the inside. Every window was sealed shut. No trace of forced entry was observed anywhere on the grounds.

Yet Mr. Wynn lay motionless in his kitchen, a glass of water overturned beside his chair, a half-eaten sandwich resting on the counter. No weapon was present. No visitors' footprints marred the muddy garden outside.

"This is, without exaggeration, the most peculiar case I have witnessed in thirty-two years on the force," Callahan stated. "There is no indication of foul play, no evidence of natural decline, and the gentleman simply… ceased to be."

Neighbors recall Wynn as a retired actuary who lived alone, tending an immaculate garden and reading three novels a week. "He was a quiet fellow," said Dorothy Kellerman, 74, of the adjacent lot. "Never troubled anyone. I cannot fathom what might have happened."

Detectives have collected the glass, the sandwich, and fingerprints throughout the dwelling. A medical examiner will determine the precise manner of his passing. The investigation remains open and active.

---

## REMARKS FROM THE OVAL OFFICE
### *A Critique by the Commander-in-Chief*

My fellow Americans — I have just been briefed on a piece that appeared in the Daily Chronicle, and I wish to speak to it briefly, because our nation demands honesty from its institutions, including the press.

First — and I say this with the full gravity of the office I hold — we owe Gerald Wynn more than a three-paragraph dispatch with no answers. This is a man. This is a neighbor. This is a citizen who deserved to be safe behind his own locked door, the very sanctuary this republic was built to guarantee.

Now. The reporting? Competent, I will grant. Callahan's quote is vivid. The detail about the sealed windows and bolted entrance paints a picture that chills the spine. And Mrs. Kellerman — God bless her — she captures the grief of a small community in a single sentence. I respect that craftsmanship.

But here is where I must push back, and I will not equivocate. *Three paragraphs.* Three. For a matter this tangled. Where is the medical examiner's preliminary timeline? Where is the question of whether the glass was touched by another hand? Where is the broader inquiry into whether this was truly without reason — or whether the investigation has declared its own mystery before the ink on the first report is dry?

And I will tell you something. The media moves fast. Too fast. They package sorrow into a headline, sell confusion like a product on a shelf, and pivot by Tuesday. I have sat in this very chair where decisions are made for this nation, and I can tell you plainly: the truth of a matter often arrives on the fourth or fifth day, not the first. The public deserves the full picture. Not a snapshot. Not a riddle sold as journalism.

I will not rest until every citizen feels secure behind their own door, in their own home. That is a promise. That is a vow. And I will honor it.

God bless Gerald Wynn. God bless this nation. And God bless you — every last one.

The rain hammered against the broken window of the abandoned garage where Miso had been sleeping for three days. He remembered the warm hands that used to stroke his orange fur, the laughter of a little girl named Lily who called him "Miso" because of his golden coloring. *But that was before the moving truck came, before the cardboard boxes swallowed their home, and before the door slammed shut behind the last of his beloved humans.* Miso had been outside in the garden when the family left in a hurry. By the time he bounded back through the cat flap, the house was empty. *The silence inside those familiar rooms had been the loudest sound he had ever heard.* Now, three weeks later, he wandered the streets of a town that no longer recognized him. His once-glossy coat was matted with mud and burrs. His ribs pressed against his skin like the bars of a cage. Every night, he curled beneath parked cars and dreamed of the kitchen floor where Lily used to spill her milk for him to lap up. *He missed the sound of her small feet pattering across the tiles at dawn.*

On the twenty-second day, Miso found himself near the old oak tree where his family used to have picnics. A strange woman sat beneath the branches, reading a book with a cup of tea resting on her knee. Miso approached cautiously, his nose twitching at the scent of chamomile and something older, something like grief. The woman looked up, and her eyes softened when she saw the trembling orange cat. "Oh, you poor thing," she whispered, setting aside her book. *She reached out slowly, giving him time to retreat if he needed to.* Miso pressed his head against her trembling fingers. Her name, he would later learn, was Eleanor, and she had lost her own companion just last winter. She carried him home in her arms, and for the first time in weeks, Miso felt the steady rhythm of another heartbeat against his own. *The walk back to her small cottage was the longest journey of his life, yet it was the one he no longer had to make alone.*

Eleanor fed him tuna from a can and spoke to him in a soft, singing voice. She set up a little bed by the fireplace, and Miso curled into it with a purr that rumbled like distant thunder. He did not forget Lily, and he never would. *On certain evenings, when the rain tapped the windows just right, Miso would gaze out at the dark street and remember.* But the memory no longer cut him like a blade. It was softer now, like a song played on a distant radio. Eleanor had a way of filling the spaces that grief left behind. She talked to him about her garden, about the roses she was trying to grow back after a long illness. Miso would stretch and yawn, as if offering his approval.

One morning, a delivery arrived at Eleanor's doorstep. Inside the package was a small hand-drawn picture of an orange cat with a bow tie. On the back, in childish letters, it simply said that Lily was sorry and loved him forever. Eleanor read the note aloud, and Miso sat very still, his ears rotating like small satellite dishes. *He understood, in some wordless cat-language way, that he was still loved.* He purred louder than he had in weeks and rubbed his cheek against the drawing. Eleanor smiled and tucked the picture into the pocket of her cardigan. That evening, she made a plate of salmon and placed it on the kitchen floor, right where Miso could reach it. The old kitchen felt different from the one he had lost, yet something about it felt like a beginning rather than an ending. *Miso ate every last flake of salmon and then curled in a sunbeam on the windowsill.*

Outside, the world moved on, as it always did. But here, in this small cottage with its mismatched cups and its single human companion, the cat had found a rhythm again. He was not the cat he had been when the family moved away. *He was older in the ways that mattered—warier, softer, braver.* And when Eleanor scratched behind his ears that night, Miso closed his eyes and let himself be held. The orphaned cat slept deeply, and for the first time, his dreams contained no empty rooms. They contained roses, and tea, and a small hand reaching down from a great height. *Tomorrow would be another day, and that was enough.*

# 🐘 The Bit Quiz: How Well Do You Know Your Elephants? 🐘

**Instructions:** Answer each question below. Good luck — and try not to panic like an **elephant** staring at a tiny mouse!

---

**1.** How many bits are in one byte?
a) 4
b) 8
c) 16
d) 32

**2.** In binary, what does a single "bit" represent?
a) A choice between red and blue
b) A choice between 0 and 1
c) A choice between 0 and 9
d) The size of an **elephant's** footprint in binary form

**3.** How many bits are needed to represent 256 unique values?
a) 4
b) 6
c) 8
d) 12

**4.** What is the decimal value of the binary number `1101`?
a) 11
b) 13
c) 15
d) 14

**5.** The XOR (exclusive OR) gate outputs 1 only when:
a) Both inputs are 1
b) The inputs are different
c) The inputs are the same
d) An **elephant** sneezes near the circuit board

**6.** How many bits does a nibble contain?
a) 1
b) 2
c) 4
d) 8

**7.** A 32-bit processor can address up to how many bytes of memory?
a) 65,536
b) 2,147,483,648
c) 4,294,967,296
d) 256

**8.** In a 4-bit binary number, what is the largest value representable?
a) 4
b) 15
c) 31
d) 16

---

## Answer Key

1. **b) 8**
2. **b) A choice between 0 and 1**
3. **c) 8** (2⁸ = 256)
4. **b) 13** (8+4+0+1)
5. **b) The inputs are different**
6. **c) 4**
7. **c) 4,294,967,296** (2³² bytes ≈ 4 GB)
8. **b) 15** (2⁴ − 1)

---

**Scoring:**
- 8/8: You've got more bits than an **elephant** has legs — brilliant!
- 5–7: Solid effort, you binary brain!
- Below 5: Time to rewire those circuits. 🐘

*Good luck on your next exam — or your next encounter with an actual elephant!*

# How to Improve Your Writing Skills

Writing is a skill that EVERY person can develop. Whether you are drafting emails, crafting stories, or building reports, your ability to communicate on paper shapes how others perceive your ideas. The good news is that meaningful improvement is entirely within your reach, regardless of where you are starting from today.

***

Three essential habits will set you on the right path. Here are the core strategies to focus on:

* Read widely and often, exposing yourself to different styles, tones, and structures so that your own voice grows richer and more versatile over time.
* Edit ruthlessly and CONSISTENTLY after every writing session, cutting filler words and tightening your sentences until only the strongest, clearest language remains.
* Seek honest feedback from trusted readers who will point out blind spots and awkward phrasing that you simply cannot see in your own work.

***

Consistency matters far more than intensity. Writing for just twenty minutes each day builds momentum and confidence in ways that a single marathon session never will. Keep a journal, start a personal blog, or rewrite old drafts from scratch. The act of showing up regularly trains your brain to find the right words more easily and reduces the fear of the blank page.

***

Remember that every celebrated author was once a nervous beginner staring at an empty document. Progress will feel slow at times, but each sentence you craft brings you closer to clarity and precision. Trust the process, stay curious about language, and let your unique voice emerge naturally through steady, patient practice.

resps:
# The Kitchen After

The last time all the cousins gathered in this kitchen, the linoleum was still yellow and the refrigerator still had the magnet shaped like a watermelon.

Now Marcus stood at the counter in his work shirt, sleeves rolled to the elbows, stirring a pot of soup because no one else would. Across the room, his cousins—his actual, literal, childhood cousins—argued about whether to split the grocery bill by share or by portion. Thirty-one years old, and they were still negotiating like kids over the last juice box.

"I just want to sit down," said Lena, leaning against the doorframe in a suit she'd worn to a funeral three days ago. "Can we just *eat*?"

Marcus poured five bowls. Five. Because the cousins numbered five again—had been five for thirty years—but the chair at the head of the table sat empty, where their mother used to preside like a small, furious queen.

They ate in a silence that was not quite silence. It was the sound of chewing and swallowing and pretending the empty chair was just a chair.

At eleven, Marcus would have cried. At eleven, the cousins would have thrown peas at each other and declared the whole evening boring. Now they ate their soup and talked about mortgages, about the slow erosion of friendships, about what it meant to be the last two who remembered the smell of their mother's kitchen in summer.

"You okay?" Lena asked him.

He shrugged. "The soup's a little salty."

She laughed. He almost smiled.

They washed the dishes together, five cousins in a small kitchen, passing plates like a bucket brigade. Nobody made a speech. Nobody said *this is what growing up is*. They just dried the bowls, stacked them, and turned off the yellowed lights one by one.

Outside, the cars started up. Five taillights in the dark, pulling away in different directions.

When considering the likelihood of encountering a dog at either a beach or a park, the answer becomes quite clear once we examine the various social, legal, and practical factors that govern these two environments. Between the two locations I visited during my outing, the park stands as the far more probable setting for spotting a dog. This conclusion is not drawn from a single observation but rather from a constellation of reasons that collectively paint a very clear picture of why canine companions flock to green spaces with such regularity.

Parks have been, for generations, designed with the explicit intention of serving as recreational areas where people can bring their pets. Walk through any neighborhood park in a typical city, and within minutes you will spot dogs of every breed and size being led along winding paths, playing on grassy expanses, or simply resting in the shade of mature oak and maple trees. Many municipal parks go further by installing fenced enclosures specifically labeled as dog areas, complete with separate sections for small and large breeds, waste stations, and sometimes even agility equipment. These purpose-built spaces are a testament to how thoroughly parks embrace canine visitors as welcome members of the community gathering there.

Beaches, by contrast, operate under an entirely different set of expectations and regulations. While some coastal towns do permit dogs on the sand during specific hours or in designated zones, a large number of beaches maintain strict no-dog policies throughout the year, and many enforce seasonal bans during the summer months when visitor numbers peak. The reasoning behind these restrictions is multifaceted. Beachgoers expect clean sand free of animal waste, they desire unobstructed space for swimming and sunbathing, and they often express concerns about hygiene and safety when large or energetic dogs share the shoreline with children and sunbathers. The local ordinances in many seaside communities explicitly prohibit pets on the beach between certain dates, sometimes as early as the first of May and lasting through the end of September. These legal frameworks drastically reduce the statistical probability of seeing a dog at a beach compared to a park.

The physical environment of a park also aligns remarkably well with a dog's needs and a owner's desire for comfortable companionship during an outing. Parks offer shaded pathways, which protect both human and canine from the punishing heat of midday sun. They contain benches where owners can sit and relax while their four-legged friends sniff around nearby grass and undergrowth. Many parks feature ponds, streams, or sprinkler systems where a dog can cool its paws and tongue on a warm afternoon. The soft, yielding grass provides a gentle surface for paws, a significant improvement over hot sand or rough pebbles. Additionally, the trees, shrubs, and flower beds in a park create a landscape of fascinating scents that engage a dog's powerful sense of smell, keeping the animal mentally stimulated and content while its owner enjoys the surroundings.

Beaches present challenges that make them less appealing to many dog owners. Sand gets into fur, ears, and paws in ways that are difficult to clean afterward. The intense ultraviolet radiation reflecting off the water and sand can scorch sensitive paw pads and skin. Salt water, while tempting for a thirsty animal, can cause stomach upset if ingested in quantity. There is often no immediate source of fresh, cool water at a beach, whereas parks typically maintain drinking fountains and shaded areas. The social dynamics of a beach also differ; people there tend to seek quiet relaxation and solitude on their towels, and the presence of an unfamiliar, energetic dog can disrupt that peace in ways that feel less intrusive in a park, where movement and activity are the norm.

The social culture surrounding parks reinforces their status as dog-friendly domains. Park goers generally anticipate encountering all sorts of animals, from squirrels and birds to the occasional rabbit, and adding a dog to this menagerie feels entirely natural. Conversations between strangers often begin with a compliment or question about someone's dog while walking along a trail or waiting near a playground. Dogs at parks serve as social catalysts, bringing people together for short chats about training, breeds, and favorite local treats. The atmosphere of a park accommodates this energy and unpredictability in a way that a quiet beach, where someone might be reading a novel under a parasol, simply does not.

From a purely statistical standpoint, the numbers strongly support the park as the more likely location. In any given metropolitan area, there are typically dozens of public parks spread across residential neighborhoods, accessible to the millions of households that own dogs. A city might have only a handful of public beaches, and those beaches are often located on the periphery, requiring a longer journey to reach. The sheer accessibility and abundance of parks mean that a dog owner can step outside, cross a street or two, and arrive at a green space within minutes of deciding to take their pet out. This convenience factor cannot be overstated, and it translates directly into higher frequency of dog presence in parks versus beaches.

Furthermore, the types of activities that dogs and their owners engage in differ greatly between the two settings. At a park, a dog can walk, explore, play fetch with a ball or frisbee among the trees, socialize with other dogs in a controlled manner, and enjoy the changing terrain of hills, stairs, and bridges. These activities satisfy the exercise and enrichment needs of most dog breeds without requiring vast open stretches of sand and surf. At a beach, the primary activities center on swimming in the ocean, which many dog owners actually discourage due to concerns about strong currents, jellyfish, and the ingestion of salt water. This limits the practical reasons a dog owner would choose a beach over the park just down the road.

Taking all of these considerations together—the permissive legal landscape of parks, the restrictive nature of beach regulations, the physical comfort a park provides for animals, the social acceptance of dogs in green spaces, the numerical advantage of parks in any urban or suburban area, and the range of enriching activities available to canines on grass rather than sand—the conclusion is unmistakable. The park I visited during my outing was, without question, the location where encountering a dog was far more likely. The beach, while occasionally hosting a lucky canine visitor who has beaten the rules or caught an off-season window, simply does not match the park's reputation as the everyday companion destination for the millions of dogs living alongside us in our communities.

Does this make sense?

# How to Conduct a Job Interview

A well-conducted job interview is one of the most important steps in building a strong team. Whether you're a seasoned hiring manager or interviewing for the first time, having a clear structure and thoughtful approach can make all the difference in identifying the right candidate. This guide walks you through every stage of the process.

## Before the Interview: Preparation Is Everything

The most successful interviews happen long before the candidate walks through the door. Start by reviewing the job description thoroughly and identifying the key competencies, skills, and personality traits you need. From there, develop a structured set of questions that will help you evaluate each candidate consistently.

Prepare a mix of question types:

- **Behavioral questions:** "Tell me about a time when [question about handling a workplace conflict]." These reveal how a candidate has navigated real challenges in the past.
- **Situational questions:** "If you were assigned a project with a deadline that seemed impossible, what would you do?" These test problem-solving instincts.
- **Technical or role-specific questions:** These verify that the candidate possesses the hard skills the role demands.
- **Cultural-fit questions:** "What kind of team environment brings out your best work?" These help gauge alignment with your company values.

Compile your questions into a scoring rubric so that every candidate is evaluated on the same criteria. This reduces unconscious bias and makes your final hiring decision more objective.

## Setting the Stage

On the day of the interview, make sure the environment is comfortable and professional. Book a quiet room, silence notifications on your devices, and have the candidate's résumé and your question sheet ready. Greet the candidate warmly by name, offer water, and briefly explain the structure of the interview. Letting them know the agenda—"We'll spend about 15 minutes on your background, 20 minutes on role-specific questions, and 10 minutes for you to ask us questions"—eases nervousness and sets expectations.

## During the Interview: Listen More Than You Speak

The golden rule of interviewing is the 80/20 principle: the candidate should be doing roughly 80% of the talking. Your role is to guide the conversation, probe deeper when answers are vague, and resist the urge to fill silences. If a candidate says, "I managed a successful project," follow up with, "What made it successful? What specific role did you play? What went wrong along the way?"

Take notes throughout, but maintain eye contact and an engaged posture. Avoid leading questions that telegraph the "right" answer. Instead of asking, "You're comfortable working in a fast-paced environment, right?" try, "Describe a time when you had to juggle multiple competing priorities. What did that look like?"

A helpful placeholder technique is to keep a set of follow-up prompts ready. For example, if a candidate's answer is incomplete, you can ask, "Could you give me a more concrete example of [topic they mentioned]?" This keeps the conversation flowing naturally without putting the candidate on the spot.

## Red Flags to Watch For

Pay attention to how candidates speak about former employers and colleagues. Consistently blaming others, speaking with bitterness about a previous manager, or being unable to articulate any lessons learned from a failure can signal deeper issues. Equally, watch for candidates who deflect questions with generalities and never circle back to a specific instance.

That said, nervousness is normal. Distinguish between genuine inexperience in communication and a poor attitude. Give candidates a moment to collect their thoughts before moving on.

## The Candidate's Questions: Don't Skip This

Reserve the final five to ten minutes for the candidate to ask questions. The quality of their questions often reveals their level of interest and preparation. A candidate who asks about team dynamics, growth opportunities, or the metrics used to measure success in the role is showing engagement. One who has no questions at all may not be as invested.

## After the Interview: Act Quickly and Thoughtfully

Within 24 hours of the interview, write down your impressions while they're fresh. Note specific examples the candidate gave, your gut reactions, and how their answers mapped onto your rubric. If you interviewed with a panel, schedule a debrief within a day or two to align on feedback before memories fade or bias sets in.

Communicate your decision to the candidate in a timely, respectful manner. Even a rejection delivered promptly and kindly leaves a positive impression of your company.

## Final Thoughts

# How to Conduct a Job Interview

A well-conducted job interview is one of the most important steps in building a strong team. Whether you're a seasoned hiring manager or interviewing for the first time, having a clear structure and thoughtful approach can make all the difference in identifying the right candidate. This guide walks you through every stage of the process.

## Before the Interview: Preparation Is Everything

The most successful interviews happen long before the candidate walks through the door. Start by reviewing the job description thoroughly and identifying the key competencies, skills, and personality traits you need. From there, develop a structured set of questions that will help you evaluate each candidate consistently.

Prepare a mix of question types:

- **Behavioral questions:** "Tell me about a time when [question about handling a workplace conflict]." These reveal how a candidate has navigated real challenges in the past.
- **Situational questions:** "If you were assigned a project with a deadline that seemed impossible, what would you do?" These test problem-solving instincts.
- **Technical or role-specific questions:** These verify that the candidate possesses the hard skills the role demands.
- **Cultural-fit questions:** "What kind of team environment brings out your best work?" These help gauge alignment with your company values.

Compile your questions into a scoring rubric so that every candidate is evaluated on the same criteria. This reduces unconscious bias and makes your final hiring decision more objective.

## Setting the Stage

On the day of the interview, make sure the environment is comfortable and professional. Book a quiet room, silence notifications on your devices, and have the candidate's résumé and your question sheet ready. Greet the candidate warmly by name, offer water, and briefly explain the structure of the interview. Letting them know the agenda—"We'll spend about 15 minutes on your background, 20 minutes on role-specific questions, and 10 minutes for you to ask us questions"—eases nervousness and sets expectations.

## During the Interview: Listen More Than You Speak

The golden rule of interviewing is the 80/20 principle: the candidate should be doing roughly 80% of the talking. Your role is to guide the conversation, probe deeper when answers are vague, and resist the urge to fill silences. If a candidate says, "I managed a successful project," follow up with, "What made it successful? What specific role did you play? What went wrong along the way?"

Take notes throughout, but maintain eye contact and an engaged posture. Avoid leading questions that telegraph the "right" answer. Instead of asking, "You're comfortable working in a fast-paced environment, right?" try, "Describe a time when you had to juggle multiple competing priorities. What did that look like?"

A helpful placeholder technique is to keep a set of follow-up prompts ready. For example, if a candidate's answer is incomplete, you can ask, "Could you give me a more concrete example of [topic they mentioned]?" This keeps the conversation flowing naturally without putting the candidate on the spot.

## Red Flags to Watch For

Pay attention to how candidates speak about former employers and colleagues. Consistently blaming others, speaking with bitterness about a previous manager, or being unable to articulate any lessons learned from a failure can signal deeper issues. Equally, watch for candidates who deflect questions with generalities and never circle back to a specific instance.

That said, nervousness is normal. Distinguish between genuine inexperience in communication and a poor attitude. Give candidates a moment to collect their thoughts before moving on.

## The Candidate's Questions: Don't Skip This

Reserve the final five to ten minutes for the candidate to ask questions. The quality of their questions often reveals their level of interest and preparation. A candidate who asks about team dynamics, growth opportunities, or the metrics used to measure success in the role is showing engagement. One who has no questions at all may not be as invested.

## After the Interview: Act Quickly and Thoughtfully

Within 24 hours of the interview, write down your impressions while they're fresh. Note specific examples the candidate gave, your gut reactions, and how their answers mapped onto your rubric. If you interviewed with a panel, schedule a debrief within a day or two to align on feedback before memories fade or bias sets in.

Communicate your decision to the candidate in a timely, respectful manner. Even a rejection delivered promptly and kindly leaves a positive impression of your company.

## Final Thoughts

Conducting a job interview is both a science and an art. The structure—prepared questions, a scoring rubric, a consistent flow—gives you rigor. The art lives in your curiosity, your ability to listen deeply, and your willingness to treat every candidate with respect regardless of the outcome. Invest in both, and you'll not only find the right person for the role but also build a reputation as an employer worth working for.

resps:
<<The Echoing Biotechnology Field in 2023: Resonances of Revolution>>

If 2023 were a sound, it would be a chorus. The biotechnology field that year didn't just advance—it echoed, each breakthrough reverberating into the next, creating a symphony of discovery that left researchers, investors, and patients alike stunned by the sheer momentum of progress.

CRISPR gene-editing therapies finally crossed the finish line. In December 2023, the FDA approved Casgevy, the first gene-editing treatment for sickle cell disease. It was not a whisper; it was a thunderclap whose echo reshaped how regulators, ethicists, and pharmaceutical companies thought about the future of medicine.

Meanwhile, mRNA technology, born in the urgency of a pandemic, echoed outward into oncology. Moderna and BioNTech pushed personalized cancer vaccines into mid-stage trials, carrying the platform's lessons of speed and modularity into entirely new disease territories.

AI-driven drug discovery echoed through wet labs everywhere. AlphaFold's predictions of protein structures became foundational infrastructure, and generative AI models began designing novel molecules, compressing decade-long pipelines into years.

Synthetic biology echoed into sustainability, with engineered microbes producing materials, fuels, and food ingredients at industrial scale.

The echo was everywhere. And it was beautiful.

---

**A Critique of This Blog Post**

This piece is, frankly, a glossy brochure masquerading as analysis. Here are its failures:

First, it mistakes chronology for insight. Listing four major developments with the word "echo" stapled between them is not a thesis—it's a summary. There is no argument here about *why* these echoes resonate, who amplifies them, or who remains in the silence between them.

Second, the tone is breathless and uncritical. Casgevy is presented as a pure triumph, but the post ignores the $2.2 million price tag, the grueling conditioning regimen, and the fact that access in low-income countries—where sickle cell burden is highest—remains nearly nonexistent. Calling that a "thunderclap" without acknowledging who hears it and who is deafened by cost is journalistic laziness.

Third, the metaphors are worn. "Symphony," "thunderclap," "whisper," "echo everywhere"—these are greeting-card sentiments dressed in paragraph form. The title promises an "echoing" field but delivers only a reverb effect on a press release.

Fourth, there is no engagement with the field's genuine tensions: the regulatory lag, the ethical minefield of germline editing still lingering in the background, the consolidation of biotech capital into fewer and fewer firms, or the environmental ethics of synthetic biology at scale. The post reads as if these complications simply don't exist.

Finally, the structure is predictable: four paragraphs, four domains, four adjectives. It tells me the field is important. It does not make me *understand* it.

In short, this is advocacy writing, not criticism. And the echo it produces is not revolution—it's the hollow resonance of a press conference room.

P.S. The irony of a blog post about "echoing" that echoes the most surface-level talking points of every 2023 biotech year-end roundup is, unfortunately, the most accurate metaphor in the entire piece.

arg_0: [{"role": "user", "content": "What's the difference between a 2-stroke and a 4-stroke motor? Your entire response must be in English and contain only lowercase letters."}]

resps:
a 2-stroke engine completes its power cycle in two piston strokes (one up, one down) and one crankshaft revolution. it combines intake and compression in the first stroke, and combustion and exhaust in the second stroke. it typically uses a ported cylinder for intake/exhaust rather than valves, and often requires a fuel-oil mixture since it has no separate oil reservoir (though some modern ones use separate oil injection).

a 4-stroke engine completes its power cycle in four piston strokes (two up, two down) and two crankshaft revolutions. the four strokes are: intake (piston down, air/fuel enters), compression (piston up, mixture is compressed), power (combustion pushes piston down), and exhaust (piston up, burnt gases are expelled). it uses dedicated valves for intake and exhaust.

key differences:

- power delivery: a 2-stroke fires every revolution; a 4-stroke fires every other revolution.
- complexity: 2-strokes are simpler, lighter, and have fewer moving parts (no valvetrain).
- lubrication: 2-strokes burn oil mixed with fuel; 4-strokes have a dedicated oil sump.
- emissions: 2-strokes are generally dirtier because unburned fuel escapes with exhaust; 4-strokes burn fuel more completely.
- fuel efficiency: 4-strokes are typically more fuel-efficient.
- maintenance: 2-strokes need more frequent oil mixing and have shorter lifespans under heavy use.
- weight and cost: 2-strokes are cheaper and lighter for the same displacement.

common uses: 2-strokes are found in chainsaws, small outboards, dirt bikes, and small generators. 4-strokes dominate cars, motorcycles, and larger engines.

doc.prompt: What are the steps to be followed for the documentation of a GM in SAP? Just list the steps without saying the word steps or step.

arg_0: [{"role": "user", "content": "What are the steps to be followed for the documentation of a GM in SAP? Just list the steps without saying the word steps or step."}]

resps:
1. Identify the relevant movement type (e.g., 101 – Goods Receipt, 201 – Goods Issue to cost center, 261 – Scrapping, 311 – Storage location transfer, etc.).

2. Launch the appropriate transaction code in SAP: **MIGO** (Goods Movement), **MB1A** (Goods Issue), **MB1B** (Transfer Posting), **MB1C** (Other Goods Receipt), or **MB01** (legacy).

3. Select the transaction category within the screen: Goods Receipt, Goods Issue, Transfer Posting, Return Delivery, or Stands.

4. Enter the material number, plant, storage location, and batch number (if applicable).

5. Specify the quantity and, where relevant, the entry unit or alternative unit of measure.

6. Provide the reference document or source object (purchase order number, production order, delivery note, cost center, WBS element, etc.).

7. Enter any required reason code, special stock indicator (e.g., E for sales order stock, Q for quality inspection, K for consignment), or movement reason.

8. Adjust valuation, account assignment, or additional fields if the scenario demands it (e.g., split valuation, batch determination, or automatic account determination override).

9. Review all entered data for accuracy and completeness.

10. Click **Post** (or press **Ctrl + S / Enter**) to commit the transaction.

resps:
**A Fan's Plea: The Vancouver Canucks and Environmental Mindfulness**

By Naomi

There's a specific kind of electricity that fills Rogers Arena on a game night. The roar of the crowd, the flash of blue and green jerseys, the sound of skates carving ice — it's a feeling I've carried with me for years. I love this team. I love this city. And it's exactly because of that love that I feel compelled to say something: the Vancouver Canucks need to be more mindful about the environments they inhabit and impact.

When you live in Vancouver, you live among old-growth forests, fragile coastlines, and waters still full of salmon. You grow up watching the seasons change and feeling the weather shift. You know, in your bones, that the world around you is not a backdrop — it is a living, breathing system. So why does it feel as though our hockey team hasn't fully caught up to that reality?

From the mountains of single-use plastics discarded in concession lines to the energy demands of arenas running full blast for twenty games a month, the footprint of a professional hockey season is enormous. I'm not asking for perfection. I'm asking for awareness. I'm asking for a team that wears Vancouver on its crest to treat Vancouver's ecosystems as more than just a scenic view from the rink.

And it isn't just about recycling bins. It's about the *environment* in the broader sense — the culture within the organization, the way players and staff are supported mentally and emotionally, the communities surrounding the arena that deserve investment and respect. A team that is mindful of its surroundings lifts everyone. A team that ignores them leaves gaps where connection and responsibility should be.

I see what other franchises have done — sustainability partnerships, community garden initiatives, mental health resources embedded into the locker room culture. The Canucks have the platform, the media market, and the passionate fanbase to lead. Imagine what it would mean for thousands of kids in British Columbia to watch their favourite players championing clean waterways or showing up to plant trees along the North Shore. Imagine the ripple effect of a captain saying, "This is our home. Let's take care of it."

I don't write this as an enemy of the franchise. I write it as a fan who believes this team is capable of being more than a game. I believe they can be stewards.

So here's my hope for the next season: less complacency, more intention. Less greenwashing in a press release, more green action in the parking lot and the practice facility and the neighborhoods nearby. Be mindful. Be present. Be Vancouver.

I'm still in the stands. I still believe. I just need the team to believe alongside me.

Naomi thanks you for reading.

First repeat the request word for word without change, then give your answer. Do not say any word before repeating the request.

**Riddle:**

I am denoted by ∫. I am the sum that never sums. Slice me into pieces of *dx*, and I reveal the curve from which I was born. I am the antonym of d/dx. I gather scattered *f(x)* into one elegant *F(x)*. What am I?

**Answer:** The integral (antiderivative).

*Explanation:* The integral symbol ∫ gathers infinitely many tiny slices (*dx*) of a function *f(x)* back into the original function *F(x)* from which it was derived — the reverse operation of differentiation, d/dx.

Other Chinese surnames romanized as "Jiang" include 姜 (ginger) and 蒋 (a separate surname), so the pinyin alone doesn't uniquely identify the character.

- **Xiang** (湘/祥/香) – shares the "-iang" sound pattern
- **Liang** (梁/亮/良) – similar ending sound, meaning "beam" or "bright/good"
- **Jiang** (蒋) – a distinct Chinese surname with the same pinyin
- **Zhang** (章/张) – often confused with Jiang by non-native speakers

These all share the "-ang" or "-iang" phonetic pattern common in Mandarin.

resps:
Poem 1

A Splash of Color on the Crown

There was a morning when the mirror showed me
not the same old shade I'd worn for years,
but something electric, something bold and new—
a violet cascade tumbling past my ears,
a crimson fire that caught the kitchen light
and turned an ordinary Tuesday into a festival.

Oh, the joy of it! The way the strangers smile
and point at your head as if you've hung a lantern
on your shoulders for the whole street to follow.
The way you tilt your chin just slightly up
beneath the fluorescent buzz of the grocery store,
because today your hair is a declaration,
a neon sign that reads: *I am not finished yet.*

And the rinsing! God, the rinsing of it—
the tub running pink and plum, the bathroom
looking like a sunset drowned in porcelain,
your fingers tangled in a silk of something
you chose, you *decided*, you built with your own hands
from a box and a pair of gloves and stubborn will.

There is no permission needed here, no committee,
no tradition passed down through generations
of muted browns and careful, quiet grays.
There is only you, a plastic cape, a timer,
and the wild, childlike thrill of saying,
"Today I am the color of a bruised plum,
and that is *enough*. That is everything."

******

Poem 2

The Blue-Green Confession

I walked into the salon feeling like a sentence
that hadn't found its verb, just a noun
sitting heavy on a page, waiting for some action.

Then she swirled the bowl and I watched
the brush drag cobalt and emerald
across strands that had only ever known
the dull beige of being overlooked.

And when she rinsed and blow-dried,
and I saw myself with a waterfall
of sea-foam and midnight crashing
over my collarbones, I laughed. Actually laughed,
the way you do when you're six
and someone finally lets you
paint with the whole box of crayons.

Now I catch my reflection in café windows
and wink at myself like a co-conspirator.
Now strangers stop me on the sidewalk
and say, "Love the hair!" and I say,
"Thank you, I *chose* it,"
and the choosing is the whole damn miracle.

It isn't vanity. Or maybe it is,
but the good kind—the kind that says
my body is a canvas and I refuse
to leave it blank for someone else to fill.
It's the green of new leaves in April,
the blue of a sky you thought was just
a boring gray until the clouds split open.

I step outside. The wind picks up
and flings my color across my face
like a flag, like a dare, like a song
I've been humming under my breath
my whole life, and now, finally,
am brave enough to sing out loud.

वर्तमान आर्थिक संकट और पर्यावरण पर इसका प्रभाव

वर्तमान समय में विश्व अनेक आर्थिक चुनौतियों से जूझ रहा है। महंगाई, बेरोजगारी, आपूर्ति श्रृंखला में अराजकता और कच्चे माल की कीमतों में वृद्धि ने न केवल मनुष्यों की जीवनशैली को प्रभावित किया है, बल्कि पर्यावरण पर भी इसका गहरा और बहुआयामी प्रभव पड़ा है।

आर्थिक संकट का सबसे प्रत्यक्ष प्रभाव क्लाइमेट या जलवायु पर पड़ा है। जब सरकारों के पास बजट की कमी होती है, तो पर्यावरण संरक्षण के लिए आवंटित धन सबसे पहले काटा जाता है। क्लाइमेट परिवर्तन से निपटने के लिए बनाई गई योजनाएँ, वृक्षारोपण कार्यक्रम और प्रदूषण नियंत्रण के उपाय अक्सर टल जाते हैं। इससे वायुमंडल में ग्रीन हाउस गैसों का स्तर बढ़ता जाता है और जलवायु संकट और भी गहराता जाता है।

एनर्जी क्षेत्र पर इस संकट का गहरा असर दिखाई देता है। जब एनर्जी की कीमतें आसमान छूती हैं, तो गरीब देश और जनता सस्ती, लेकिन अस्वच्छ ईंधन जैसे कोयले और लकड़ी पर लौट आती है। इससे वायु प्रदूषण बढ़ता है और कार्बन उत्सर्जन में वृद्धि होती है। दूसरी ओर, एनर्जी के क्षेत्र में निवेश की कमी के कारण नवीकरणीय ऊर्जा परियोजनाएँ पीछे छूट जाती हैं। ग्रीन एनर्जी जैसे सौर ऊर्जा और पवन ऊर्जा के प्रोजेक्ट आर्थिक दबाव के कारण स्थगित हो जाते हैं।

यद्यपि ग्रीन अर्थव्यवस्था की दिशा में वैश्विक कदम उठाए गए थे, परंतु आर्थिक मंदी ने इस ग्रीन परिवर्तन की गति को धीमा कर दिया है। ग्रीन टेक्नोलॉजी पर शोध और विकास में कटौती हुई है। साथ ही, कुछ मामलों में आर्थिक संकट ने एक विरोधाभासी प्रभाव भी डाला है—कम उत्पादन के कारण कुछ अवधि में प्रदूषण स्तर में अस्थायी कमी आई है, परंतु यह दीर्घकालिक समाधान नहीं है।

निष्कर्षतः, आर्थिक संकट और पर्यावरण संरक्षण एक दूसरे से गहराई से जुड़े हुए हैं। सरकारों को यह समझना होगा कि पर्यावरण की उपेक्षा दीर्घकालिक आर्थिक हानि का कारण बनेगी। ग्रीन नीतियों को आर्थिक पुनर्वास का केंद्र बनाना अत्यंत आवश्यक है, ताकि क्लाइमेट परिवर्तन और आर्थिक विकास एक साथ संभव हो सकें।

resps:
<<SRE란 무엇인가>>

SRE(Site Reliability Engineering, 사이트 신뢰성 엔지니어링)는 소프트웨어 엔지니어링 원칙을 인프라 및 운영 관리에 적용하여 대규모 분산 시스템의 가용성, 성능 및 확장성을 보장하는 실무 분야입니다.

SRE의 핵심은 'management' 개념에 있습니다. 운영을 반복적인 작업에서 시스템적 접근으로 전환하여, 수동 대응을 최소화하고 자동화된 도구를 통해 시스템 전반의 상태를 'management'하는 데 중점을 둡니다.

SRE 팀은 명확한 'objective'를 설정합니다. 이 'objective'는 시스템의 가용성, 지연 시간, 처리량, 에러율 등 서비스 수준 목표(SLO)를 포함하여, 서비스가 반드시 달성해야 하는 기준을 정의합니다. 이 'objective'에 기반하여 SRE는 시스템 개선 우선순위를 결정합니다.

또한 SRE는 'indicator'를 활용하여 시스템의 건강 상태를 상시 모니터링합니다. 오류 예산(error budget)이라는 개념도 중요한 'indicator'로 작용하며, 이를 통해 개발과 운영 사이의 균형을 유지합니다.

결국 SRE는 신뢰성 있는 소프트웨어 시스템을 설계하고, 유지하며, 개선하는 데 특화된 엔지니어링 학문이자 실천 방법론입니다.
